lanes.lane: Complex front-end / visual web (landing pages, portfolios, scroll animation, WebGL, design-to-code, UI cloning, a11y)

items.name: LMArena / arena.ai Code Arena - WebDev leaderboard
items.what_it_tests: Building real web UIs/apps from a prompt, now including agentic coding workflows. Judged by blind human preference.
items.example_task: User prompt such as 'build a portfolio site for a photographer with a parallax hero'. Two anonymous models build it and the user votes on the rendered results.
items.how_graded: Blind pairwise human votes turned into Bradley-Terry (Elo-style) scores with CIs. As of 2026-09-25: 134 models, ~795k votes.
items.fits_our_harness: The leaderboard can't be copied, but the format can. Freeze 3-5 prompts written in the arena style, render each run's output to a screenshot or video, and run a blind pairwise AI judge (majority vote) plus optional human votes. Rank models with Bradley-Terry across Josh's runs. The arena Elo is a public reference to sanity-check his ranking against. Top of the board spreads ~1827 (claude-opus-5.5-max) to ~1656 at #10, with CIs of +/-7-18, so it is not saturated.

items.name: Design Arena (designarena.ai) - Website, UI component, 3D, Data viz, SVG, Agentic Web Dev boards
items.what_it_tests: Visual and design quality across many categories: websites, slides, mobile apps, 3D (Three.js/WebGL/shaders), data viz, UI components, SVG, logos. 'Agentic Web Dev' compares deployed React apps built by long-horizon agents.
items.example_task: The same creative prompt ('landing page for a coffee roaster with scroll-triggered reveals') goes to several models. Voters run a ~5-match mini bracket.
items.how_graded: Crowdsourced blind pairwise votes, Bradley-Terry ratings (Rating = 400*log10(strength)), refreshed every 2h, with adaptive model selection. Methodology is published.
items.fits_our_harness: Good source of category taxonomy and prompt style. Pick one prompt per category (website, 3D scene, data-viz dashboard, UI component) as frozen tasks and grade with the same blind pairwise AI-judge setup. The 3D board is described as the most demanding category (GPT-6 Astra 1474, Claude Fable 5.1 1421, Kimi K3 1420 per a third-party aggregator), which fits Josh's finding that the voxel game separates models.

items.name: UI-Bench (text-to-app visual design, expert pairwise)
items.what_it_tests: Visual excellence of AI text-to-app tools (Lovable/v0/Bolt-type tools and models): polish, hierarchy, aesthetics of generated sites.
items.example_task: One of 30 public prompts, e.g. a SaaS landing page. Each tool generates a site and design experts compare pairs.
items.how_graded: Blinded expert pairwise comparisons (4,000+ judgments on 300 sites), TrueSkill ranking with confidence intervals, based on Thurstone/adaptive comparative judgment.
items.fits_our_harness: Strong fit for the 'correct answer defined by others' principle: the prompt set and evaluation framework are open-sourced. Freeze 3-5 UI-Bench prompts verbatim. The artifact is the built site plus full-page screenshots at 3 breakpoints. The grader is a blind pairwise AI judge using UI-Bench's rubric, with TrueSkill across runs. Deterministic gates can run first: site builds, zero console errors, Lighthouse, axe.

items.name: Design2Code family (Design2Code, Sketch2Code, Figma2Code) - screenshot/sketch/Figma to code
items.what_it_tests: Faithfully reproducing a given design (real webpage screenshot, hand-drawn wireframe, or Figma file with metadata/assets) as HTML/CSS. Figma2Code adds responsiveness and code maintainability.
items.example_task: Given a screenshot of a real webpage from the dataset, write a single HTML file that renders identically. Figma2Code: given a Figma file (213 designer-curated cases), produce production UI code.
items.how_graded: Automatic visual metrics: CLIP similarity, block-match (Jonker-Volgenant aligned visual blocks), text Sorensen-Dice, CIEDE2000 color distance, position similarity, plus CW-SSIM/TreeBLEU. Sketch2Code adds layout similarity and a simulated-user multi-turn mode.
items.fits_our_harness: Easiest fully scripted visual task. The answer key is the reference screenshot plus the reference HTML (public dataset). The grader renders the output in Playwright at fixed viewport and computes SSIM/CLIP/block-match. Plain Design2Code static pages look close to saturated for frontier models (likely, not verified this session). Figma2Code (ICLR 2026) still reports gaps in responsiveness and maintainability, so prefer it or a hard Design2Code subset scored at 3 breakpoints.

items.name: WebVR - webpage recreation from VIDEO (motion, timing, transitions)
items.what_it_tests: The closest benchmark to 'scroll-driven animation / special effects'. A model watches a demo video of a webpage and recreates its interaction flow, timing, and motion continuity, not just the static look.
items.example_task: Given a screen recording of a page with scroll reveals, hover transitions and an animated hero (175 synthesized pages), rebuild it so the motion matches.
items.how_graded: Fine-grained, human-aligned visual rubric scored by an MLLM judge (96% agreement with human preference). 19 models tested; the paper reports 'substantial gaps in recreating fine-grained style and motion quality'.
items.fits_our_harness: Excellent fit for the landing-page-with-animations idea. The dataset and eval toolkit are released. Freeze 3-5 WebVR videos plus their rubrics. The artifact is the rebuilt page. The grader records a Playwright scroll-through video or frame strip of the output and has a blind AI judge score it against the frozen rubric next to the reference video. Deterministic probes can be added (see techniques).

items.name: Interaction2Code (ASE 2025) - interactive prototype to webpage
items.what_it_tests: Generating the dynamic interactions of a page (hover, click, toggle, modal, tab states) from before/after prototype screenshots, not only the static layout.
items.example_task: Given 127 pages / 374 interactions: screenshots of page state A and state B plus action.json ('click element X'), implement a page that transitions A->B on that action.
items.how_graded: Render, perform the action scripted from action.json, then compare the post-interaction screenshot with the reference using visual similarity metrics. Leaderboard on the project page.
items.fits_our_harness: Very harness-friendly. The answer key is the reference state images plus action.json (public on HF/GitHub). The grader is a Playwright script: load, screenshot, do the action, screenshot, then SSIM/CLIP against both states. A good deterministic complement to judge-graded landing pages.

items.name: ArtifactsBench (Tencent Hunyuan) - visual/interactive artifacts with temporal screenshots
items.what_it_tests: Holistic quality of generated visual artifacts across 9 categories: web apps, games, SVG, simulations, data science, management systems, multimedia editing, quick tools. Includes dynamic behavior.
items.example_task: One of 1,825 queries, e.g. 'build an interactive pomodoro timer with animated progress ring'.
items.how_graded: Programmatic render plus timed sequence of screenshots to capture animation/dynamics. An MLLM judge scores them with a per-task fine-grained checklist (>94% agreement with human preference).
items.fits_our_harness: Its per-task checklists are a ready-made public answer key for the AI-judge rung. Freeze a few web-app/animation tasks with their checklists. The grader is Playwright temporal screenshots (t=0, 1s, 3s, after interaction) plus a blind majority-vote judge against the checklist. The temporal-screenshot method is directly reusable for scroll/animation tasks.

items.name: Web-Bench (ByteDance) - 50 sequential web projects x 20 tasks, Playwright-graded
items.what_it_tests: Real front-end engineering over a long sequence: DOM, Flexbox/Grid layout, Canvas, SVG, React/Vue/Angular, state libraries, Vite/Webpack, Next.js. Each project is ~4-8 senior-engineer hours.
items.example_task: Project with 20 dependent tasks: task 1 lays out a 3-section page, later tasks add grid behavior, a canvas chart, and so on. Each task must pass its own Playwright E2E tests without breaking earlier ones.
items.how_graded: Playwright E2E tests per task (positioning, sizing, layout behavior), Pass@1. SOTA at release was only 25.1% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet with their Web-Agent).
items.fits_our_harness: Near-perfect fit: frozen spec plus public Playwright tests is exactly the top rung of Josh's ladder. Take 1-2 CSS/Canvas/SVG 'Web Standards' projects, give the whole 20-task sequence as one agentic run, and score by the number of tasks whose tests pass (a gradient, not pass/fail). Current frontier numbers weren't found; the 25% figure is from May 2025, so re-measure.

items.name: WebGen-Bench (NeurIPS 2025 D&B) - multi-file websites from scratch, agent-executed test cases
items.what_it_tests: Building a working multi-file site from an NL spec: content presentation, user interaction, data management.
items.example_task: 'Build a recipe-sharing site where users can add, filter and favorite recipes.' 647 test cases over the instruction set.
items.how_graded: Per-instruction test cases (operation + expected outcome) executed by a web-navigation agent that judges pass/fail. Best at release: Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1 at 27.8%.
items.fits_our_harness: Test cases are public on HF. Convert selected test cases into deterministic Playwright scripts where possible and let the agent-judge handle the rest. Mostly functional rather than visual; pair it with a visual judge.

items.name: WebRISE - requirement-induced state evaluation (Interaction Contract Graphs)
items.what_it_tests: Whether generated web artifacts actually implement required states and transitions, from 5 input modalities (text, markdown, sketch, image, video). Explicitly shows visual quality is not the same as functionality.
items.example_task: 442 tasks, 5,495 transitions, 5,271 requirement checks, e.g. 'from a sketch, build a multi-step form wizard with validation states'.
items.how_graded: Implementation-agnostic browser execution against Interaction Contract Graphs (observable states, user-intent transitions, DOM/visual assertions). Best model 65.6% transition validity / 66.3% requirement coverage. One model scored 80.8% on visual quality but 15.5% on transitions.
items.fits_our_harness: Its contract-graph idea is what Josh needs for animated landing pages: selector-agnostic assertions on states and transitions. Freeze a handful of tasks plus their ICGs as the answer key; the grader is a Playwright executor. Also a strong on-camera point: the prettiest page can be the most broken.

items.name: Cookie-Bench - reference-free, agent-driven interactive web evaluation
items.what_it_tests: 1,000 WebDev queries across 11 domains / 54 leaf categories and 3 difficulty tiers. Covers interactive apps and static presentation pages (landing/portfolio-type).
items.example_task: A presentation-page or interactive-app query. An evaluator agent explores the generated site while recording the screen.
items.how_graded: Cookie-Frame: static perception, then agent-driven interaction with continuous screen recording, then holistic scoring of functionality and aesthetics with failure attribution. Reports 'substantial headroom across 13 frontier LLMs'.
items.fits_our_harness: Use its query set as a source of frozen prompts, especially the static-presentation tier for landing pages. Adopt the 'recorded exploration then judge' pattern: a Playwright scroll/click walk exports a video, and a blind judge scores against a rubric. Reference-free, so no gold site is needed, but it relies more on the judge.

items.name: Cloning Bench (Vibrant Labs) - visual cloning of a real site via scripted user flow
items.what_it_tests: Agent clones a real web UI (Slack) from screenshots plus DOM snapshots, including hover states, navigation, messaging, reactions, deletion.
items.example_task: Rebuild Slack's UI in React so a 43-step 'screenplay' user flow produces matching screenshots at each checkpoint.
items.how_graded: SSIM between reference and clone screenshots at each assertion checkpoint, with pixel-diff overlays and an optional LLM pass to mask dynamic content. Mar 2026 results: Gemini 3 Pro 0.871 SSIM (but zero interactivity), Claude Opus 4.6 0.757 (full features), GLM-5 0.723, GPT-5.3 Codex 0.583.
items.fits_our_harness: The format ports cleanly even though the dataset isn't public (contact-only). Josh can build his own 'clone a public site' task: capture reference screenshots/DOM of a well-known open-source landing page at fixed viewports and scroll offsets and freeze them (hash-checked). The grader replays a scripted Playwright flow (scroll to Y, hover X, click Y) and computes per-checkpoint SSIM plus pixel-diff heatmaps, which are also great b-roll. Their Gemini result is itself a lesson: SSIM alone rewards static pixel-perfect shells, so gate with interaction assertions too.

items.name: WorldCoder-Bench (+ threejseval) - Three.js / WebGL 3D scenes
items.what_it_tests: Browser-native 3D world synthesis in Three.js: simulation, rendering, application scenarios. Loading .glb assets and obeying spatial and physical constraints. This is the WebGL hero-effect end of the lane.
items.example_task: One of 2,026 tasks, e.g. build a Three.js scene where objects fall under gravity and a click spawns a new object, with hidden behavioral contracts.
items.how_graded: StateProbe: sandboxed-browser probes of runtime Three.js state (not just pixels) against hidden, mutation-hardened contracts. Best of 9 models: 27.8% coverage on Core, 19.9% on Robust. threejseval.com is a separate public Three.js agent bench using blind human votes plus Elo plus cost/tokens (details couldn't be fetched).
items.fits_our_harness: Natural extension of the voxel game, which is the only task that already separates models. Freeze a few WorldCoder tasks. Require the scene/renderer be exposed on window (stated in the spec) so a Playwright probe can read scene graph, object positions and camera over time. Add a blind visual judge on a recorded video for aesthetics. Hard and unsaturated, with strong video appeal.

items.name: SWE-bench Multimodal (v2 open, Sep 2026) - visual front-end bug fixing in real JS repos
items.what_it_tests: Resolving real GitHub issues in JS front-end repos (UI, diagramming, data viz) where the issue includes screenshots. About 90% of instances contain visual elements.
items.example_task: 'The chart legend overlaps the axis at narrow widths (screenshot attached)': patch the repo so the hidden tests pass.
items.how_graded: Hidden unit/visual tests in Docker (FAIL_TO_PASS / PASS_TO_PASS). Original results were as low as 12.2% resolved. v2 (Sept 2026) keeps 480 reproducible tasks with flaky tests removed and rebuilt environments.
items.fits_our_harness: The answer key is the official hidden tests, which fits Josh's principle perfectly. Pick 3-5 v2 instances and run them in their Docker images. Heavier infra (Docker per repo) and less visually spectacular, but it is the 'real job' counterweight to arena-style showpieces. Current frontier scores on v2 weren't found; check swebench.com.

items.name: Accessibility of generated UIs (Microsoft a11y-llm-eval, A11YN / RealUIReq-300)
items.what_it_tests: Whether generated HTML/UI is accessible: WCAG violations, keyboard/ARIA requirements, best practices.
items.example_task: 'Build a modal dialog signup form'. It passes only with zero axe-core WCAG failures AND all requirement assertions (focus trap, labelled inputs, etc.).
items.how_graded: axe-core automated scan plus custom JS requirement/best-practice assertions, pass@k (Microsoft). A11YN uses axe-core violation counts on 300 real UI tasks. A CHI 2026 paper warns axe-optimized models can emit syntactically compliant but semantically empty attributes.
items.fits_our_harness: Best as a cheap deterministic grading layer on EVERY web task (landing pages included) rather than a standalone showpiece. Run axe-core via Playwright at 3 breakpoints, count serious/critical violations, and check keyboard reachability of every interactive element. Microsoft's test cases (prompt.yaml + test.js) can be taken verbatim as standalone frozen tasks.

items.name: Community canonical prompts - Simon Willison 'pelican riding a bicycle' SVG
items.what_it_tests: Spatial and visual reasoning expressed as code (SVG). The famous informal 'canonical community prompt'; there is an upgraded stricter version.
items.example_task: 'Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle' (or the upgraded California-brown-pelican prompt with stricter bicycle requirements).
items.how_graded: Informal human eyeballing. The prompt is public in the simonw/pelican-bicycle repo. 2026 studies ask whether labs are 'pelicanmaxxing' (contamination).
items.fits_our_harness: Cheap cold-open or palate-cleanser for videos, not a serious separator. It is likely trained on, so use Willison's upgraded prompt or a private variant with the same shape. Grade with a blind pairwise judge plus deterministic checks (valid SVG, renders, has a bicycle with 2 wheels via judge question). Very high recognition on screen.

grading_techniques: Blind pairwise preference plus Bradley-Terry/TrueSkill ranking (LMArena, Design Arena, UI-Bench): replace humans with a blind majority-vote AI judge on screenshots/videos, and optionally add Josh's own votes as a human spot-check.
Rubric/checklist MLLM-as-judge on rendered evidence, not code (ArtifactsBench per-task checklists, WebVR human-aligned visual rubric). Freeze the rubric with the task.

Temporal screenshots: capture at t=0, 0.5s, 1s, 3s and after each interaction to catch animations (ArtifactsBench). Record a full scroll-through video (Playwright recordVideo) for judge input and YouTube b-roll.

Scroll-trigger probe for scroll-driven animation: scroll to fixed offsets and assert that computed style (transform/opacity) of target elements CHANGES between offsets, and that document.getAnimations() or GSAP ScrollTrigger.getAll() is non-empty. The spec can require a stable data-attribute or class for animated sections.

Visual similarity metrics against a frozen reference: SSIM/CW-SSIM, CLIP similarity, Design2Code block-match, text Dice, CIEDE2000 color, position similarity. Pixel-diff heatmaps (Cloning Bench) as a visual explanation.
Scripted user-flow replay with per-checkpoint screenshots (Cloning Bench '43-step screenplay', Interaction2Code action.json): catches static pixel-perfect shells with zero interactivity.
Interaction Contract Graphs / state-transition assertions (WebRISE): selector-agnostic checks of observable states and transitions. Keeps grading implementation-agnostic.
Runtime state probes into canvas/WebGL (WorldCoder-Bench StateProbe): require window-exposed scene/renderer and assert object positions/physics over time, instead of pixel-only checks.
Agent-driven exploration grader (WebGen-Bench, Cookie-Bench): a browsing agent executes NL test cases. Use only where Playwright scripts can't be written.

Deterministic quality gates on every web task: build succeeds, zero console errors, Lighthouse performance/accessibility/best-practices scores with budgets (LCP, CLS, TBT), axe-core zero serious/critical violations, keyboard reachability.

Frame-rate/jank measurement during scroll: Chrome DevTools performance trace or requestAnimationFrame frame-time sampling while auto-scrolling. Assert p95 frame time under ~33ms and CLS near 0. Separates 'pretty but janky' WebGL/parallax heroes.

Responsive check: render at 375/768/1440 widths. Assert no horizontal overflow (scrollWidth <= innerWidth) and judge each breakpoint (Figma2Code finds responsiveness is where proprietary models still fail).
Hidden official tests in Docker (SWE-bench Multimodal FAIL_TO_PASS/PASS_TO_PASS) for 'real repo' front-end work.
lanes.notes:
- Frontier status is weak evidence for most academic benchmarks. Their SOTA numbers are from release time (Web-Bench 25.1% on Claude 3.7, WebGen-Bench 27.8% on DeepSeek-R1, both 2025) and I found no 2026 re-runs, so they are marked 'unknown'. Josh's own runs are the real test.
- Clearly still separating models as of Sep 2026: WebDev Arena (top-10 spread ~170 Elo, CIs +/-7-18, updated 2026-09-25), Design Arena including 3D, WebRISE (best 65.6%), WorldCoder-Bench (best 27.8%), WebVR and Cookie-Bench (both report substantial headroom), Cloning Bench (0.58-0.87 SSIM spread).
- Likely saturated: basic Design2Code static screenshot-to-HTML (inferred, not verified this session) and the pelican SVG (contaminated / 'pelicanmaxxing').
- Metric traps:
  - SSIM/CLIP reward static visual shells. In Cloning Bench Gemini 3 Pro got the highest SSIM with zero interactivity, and in WebRISE a model scored 80.8% visual but 15.5% functional. Always pair visual similarity with interaction/state assertions.
  - axe-core-optimized output can be semantically empty (CHI 2026), so add requirement assertions beyond axe.
- AI-judge caveats:
  - Arena-style votes favor flashy, dense pages and are prompt-distribution dependent.
  - LLM judges have position and self-preference bias. Randomize order, blind model identity, majority-vote over several judges, and ideally use a judge vendor different from the contestants.
  - WebVR (96%) and ArtifactsBench (>94%) report high human agreement, but on their own distributions only.
- Scroll-driven animation is the least-covered area. WebVR (video to page) is the only benchmark I found that grades motion and timing directly. Josh will likely need his own frozen task for 'portfolio with GSAP/ScrollTrigger or CSS scroll-timeline', built from a public reference page plus a WebVR-style rubric plus the deterministic scroll-trigger and jank probes above.
- Some sources were not verified in full:
  - The threejseval.com page body couldn't be fetched (title only), so its details come from the search snippet.
  - Design Arena category Elo numbers come from third-party aggregators (benchlm.ai, modelgrep.com), not the primary page.
  - Cloning Bench data is not public (contact-only).
  - SWE-bench Multimodal v2 details come from the search snippet.

lanes.lane: Real software engineering beyond toy apps: issue-fixing, feature work in existing repos, from-spec app and library builds, migrations, terminal and long-horizon agentic engineering

items.name: SWE-bench Verified (original SWE-bench family)
items.what_it_tests: Fixing real GitHub issues in popular Python repos. The agent reads the issue text and the repo, writes a patch, and hidden FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS unit tests decide the result.
items.example_task: Given a django issue and the repo checked out at the pre-fix commit, produce a patch that makes the hidden regression tests pass without breaking existing ones.
items.how_graded: Scripted: run the hidden tests inside a per-instance Docker image and record resolved or not.
items.fits_our_harness: Mechanically easy, since Harbor lists SWE-bench as a dataset and the swebench Docker harness exists. It is NOT worth a video slot. In Feb 2026 OpenAI's Frontier Evals team stopped reporting it: an audit found more than 60% of 138 problem tasks unsolvable as written, and models reproduced gold patches from the task ID alone (contamination). Use at most 1-2 instances as a calibration or sanity lane.

items.name: SWE-Bench Pro (Scale AI) and SWE-Bench Pro Verified
items.what_it_tests: Long-horizon, multi-file issue resolution and feature work across 41 professional repos in several languages. It has a public copyleft set, a private commercial set and a held-out set, which resists contamination.
items.example_task: Implement a multi-file change in a mid-size Go/TS/Python product repo from a rewritten problem statement, verified by hidden tests.
items.how_graded: Hidden unit tests in Docker, reported as resolve rate with confidence intervals. The Pro Verified follow-up (arXiv 2609.08149) adds anti-leak safeguards and fixes misleading statements and badly scoped tests; some models score 'substantially worse' after the fixes.
items.fits_our_harness: Strong fit. Pick 5-10 public instances in languages Josh cares about. The artifact is the patched repo, the answer key is the frozen hidden test files plus the Docker image digest (hash them), and the grader runs the tests. Prefer Pro Verified's corrected instances to avoid flawed-test noise. On Scale's standardized public set, the Scale leaderboard page lists Muse Spark 1.1 61.5, GPT-5.4 xHigh 59.1 and Claude Opus 4.6 thinking 51.9, so there is plenty of headroom. Vendor aggregators claim 80-90% on vendor scaffolds. That is exactly why running it yourself on a fixed harness is interesting video content.
items.recency: Released Sep 2025. Pro Verified paper Sep 2026. Leaderboard updated 2026.

items.name: SWE-bench-Live / SWE-rebench / Monthly-SWEBench (continuously refreshed issue sets)
items.what_it_tests: The same issue-to-patch skill, but on GitHub issues created after model training cutoffs. The sets refresh monthly, so they are decontaminated by construction.
items.example_task: Resolve an issue opened in July 2026 in an active Python repo (from the SWE-rebench 07-2026 split), graded by the PR's tests.
items.how_graded: Docker test execution. SWE-rebench runs 5 attempts per problem under a fixed ReAct scaffold and reports best pass@1.
items.fits_our_harness: Very good fit for the 'answer defined by other people' principle while also being contamination-proof. Pull a monthly split from Harbor Hub (swe-rebench-07-2026), freeze N tasks, and hash the tests and images. Runs locally with Docker. Every episode can use a fresh 'this month's issues' slice, which makes a good recurring video format. BenchLM's Sep 2026 page lists Opus 4.6 at about 65%, with GLM-5/5.1 about 63% (aggregator, not verified first-hand).
items.recency: Ongoing monthly through 2026 (July 2026 split on Harbor Hub).

items.name: SWE-bench Multimodal (v2)
items.what_it_tests: Issue resolution in visual/front-end JS repos where the issue includes screenshots or images (charts, maps, UI bugs), so the model must reason from visuals to code.
items.example_task: Fix a rendering bug in a JS charting library, where the issue shows a screenshot of the wrong chart.
items.how_graded: Hidden tests in Docker.
items.fits_our_harness: Good bridge between Josh's web/visual lane and real repos. The SWE-bench repo says v2 is fully open source with 480 tasks for local evaluation (per search, Sep 2026). Freeze a handful of UI-bug instances. The before/after screenshot also makes good B-roll. llm-stats lists Claude Mythos Preview at 0.590 with only 4 models evaluated, so leaderboard data is thin.
items.recency: Original late 2024. v2 open-sourced about Sep 2026 (per search snippet).

items.name: Terminal-Bench 2.0 / 2.1 (Harbor framework)
items.what_it_tests: End-to-end terminal agent work: compiling code, training models, setting up servers, sysadmin, security, data science. Each task is a Docker environment plus an instruction plus test scripts.
items.example_task: Inside a container, build a legacy C project with a broken toolchain and get its test suite green. Or configure a server so a verification script passes.
items.how_graded: Per-task test scripts run in the container after the agent finishes. 2.1 fixed 26 tasks (bugs, timeouts, reward-hacking robustness) and includes an oracle agent to validate tasks.
items.fits_our_harness: Best off-the-shelf fit. Harbor natively runs Claude Code and Codex CLI against local Docker: harbor run --dataset terminal-bench/terminal-bench-2-1 --agent claude-code --model ... Josh could either call Harbor from his runner or import task dirs (Dockerfile + tests) as frozen tasks, hashing the tests dir. Aggregators disagree on the top score: BenchLM lists GPT-5.5 at 82%, another source Claude Fable 5 at 84.3%, average about 0.57, so it is nearing the top on the best models. Use 2.1 rather than 2.0, and pick the hardest-rated tasks.

items.name: Vibe Code Bench (Vals AI)
items.what_it_tests: Building a complete, deployed web application from a natural-language spec. It covers 100 specs (50 public / 50 held-out) and 964 browser workflows with 10,131 substeps.
items.example_task: Build a multi-page web app (auth, CRUD, dashboard) from a written product spec. A browser agent then clicks through the user workflows.
items.how_graded: An autonomous browser agent executes the scripted user workflows against the running app and scores substep pass rate.
items.fits_our_harness: Maps directly onto Josh's budget-dashboard-style task, but graded by someone else's spec. Take public specs as frozen prompts. For the answer key, convert the published workflows into deterministic Playwright scripts instead of an LLM browser agent, so grading is reproducible. It is about saturated at the very top: v1.1 (updated 2026-09-22) has Claude Fable 5 at 90.35%, Opus 5.5 90.29% and Fable 5.1 90.26%, up from 41% top on v1 and 61.8% in the paper. Still separates mid-tier and open-weight models.

items.name: ViBench (Replit, CAIS 2026)
items.what_it_tests: Realistic vibe coding from production traces across 15 apps: zero-to-one app creation and feature extension, including 'Vibe-on-Vibe' (extending the model's own code).
items.example_task: Given a PRD, build a working web app. Then, as a second task, extend it with a new feature on top of the model's own output.
items.how_graded: Test plans executed against the artifact. Reports Pass@1 for fully correct artifacts and complete-failure rates.
items.fits_our_harness: Excellent fit and fully open (Apache 2.0: PRDs, test plans, scripts, harness at github.com/ViBench/vibench-public). Freeze the PRD as the prompt and the test plan as the answer key, and grade with its scripts or ported Playwright. The Vibe-on-Vibe two-stage format (build, then extend your own code) is a novel, video-friendly way to show compounding errors. Paper numbers: Opus 4.6 46% and GPT-5.2 42% Pass@1; open-weight models 12% or less; 7 of 9 degrade on vibe-on-vibe. Newer models are unmeasured.

items.name: App-Bench
items.what_it_tests: Full-stack web app building in economically important domains (healthcare, real estate, finance, legal, education), aimed at AI app-builder tools.
items.example_task: Build a clinic appointment-booking app with patient records and scheduling rules.
items.how_graded: Per its site, evaluation of the built app's functionality. Grading details not verified first-hand.
items.fits_our_harness: Useful mainly as a source of domain-realistic specs. Josh would need to write his own Playwright acceptance checks per spec unless App-Bench publishes them. Lower priority than ViBench or Vibe Code Bench, whose grading is public.

items.name: Commit0 (library generation from scratch)
items.what_it_tests: Writing an entire Python library from an API spec document plus an interactive unit-test suite. There are 54 libraries, up to 1,300 functions, with specs up to 300k tokens.
items.example_task: Given the spec docs and test suite of a mid-size library (e.g., a parsing or networking lib) with the implementation stripped, implement it until the tests pass.
items.how_graded: Fraction of the library's own unit tests passing. The agent may also use lint, type-check and coverage feedback.
items.fits_our_harness: Great 'long-horizon build to a test suite' task that runs locally (Docker; github.com/commit-0/commit0). Artifact = the implemented repo. Answer key = the library's original test suite, frozen and hashed. Grader = pytest pass fraction. Pick a small library (lite split) to keep runtime sane. Caveat: these are popular open-source libs, so memorization is a real contamination risk; prefer obscure ones or check for verbatim recall. The paper said no agent fully reproduces a library; 2026 frontier status is not re-measured in sources found.

items.name: Feature-level repo benchmarks: FeatBench, FEA-Bench, NoCode-bench
items.what_it_tests: Adding a new feature to an existing repo from a natural-language request. FEA-Bench gives function-signature hints, NoCode-bench uses doc updates as the spec, and FeatBench removes code hints entirely.
items.example_task: In a real Python repo, implement the feature described in a user-style request (no signatures given) so that the PR's new tests pass and old ones still pass.
items.how_graded: PR-derived unit tests (new feature tests + regression tests) in Docker.
items.fits_our_harness: Same recipe as SWE-bench (frozen repo commit + hidden tests), but the 'build a feature' framing makes better video than bug fixing. FeatBench is the most realistic (no hints). Freeze 3-5 instances. The papers report substantially lower resolve rates than bug-fix benchmarks, but I did not verify 2026 frontier numbers.

items.name: FreshBrew / MigrationBench (codebase migration)
items.what_it_tests: Project-level Java migration (JDK 8 to 17+) while preserving semantics. FreshBrew explicitly guards against reward hacking such as deleting tests. Repos build on JDK 8, fail on modern JDKs, and have 50% or more test coverage.
items.example_task: Migrate a real Maven project from Java 8 to Java 17 so that it builds and its original tests pass, without removing or weakening any tests.
items.how_graded: Build success on the target JDK, test pass, plus test-integrity checks (test count and coverage must not drop).
items.fits_our_harness: A distinctive, non-game 'real software' category. Artifact = the migrated repo. Answer key = the original test suite + coverage baseline (hashed). Grader = Docker with JDK 17: mvn test + test-count/coverage diff. The anti-reward-hacking check is itself good video content (did the model delete tests to pass?). The paper's best was Gemini 2.5 Flash at 54.3% of 228 repos; 2026 frontier numbers are unknown.

items.name: SWE-Lancer (Diamond public split)
items.what_it_tests: Real Upwork freelance jobs (the Expensify codebase) worth $1M in total, from $50 bug fixes to $32k features, plus 'manager' tasks choosing between implementation proposals.
items.example_task: Implement a $2,000 feature in the Expensify React Native app; graded by end-to-end tests written by professional engineers.
items.how_graded: End-to-end browser tests (Playwright) triple-verified by engineers. Score is dollars earned. Manager tasks are graded against the original hiring decision.
items.fits_our_harness: The 'dollars earned' framing is very YouTube-friendly. OpenAI open-sourced a unified Docker image + the Diamond split. Freeze a few IC SWE tasks; the answer key is their E2E tests. Caveats: the image is heavy, and Josh must first check it still builds. There is little public 2026 leaderboard activity (original paper tested Claude 3.5 Sonnet / GPT-4o / o1, none of which solved the majority), so current separation is unverified.

items.name: METR time-horizon suite (HCAST + RE-Bench + SWAA)
items.what_it_tests: Not a single task. It measures the length of task (in human-expert time) an agent can finish at 50%/80% reliability across software, ML research and cyber tasks.
items.example_task: RE-Bench-style: optimize a GPU kernel or fine-tune a model to beat a scored baseline within an 8-hour budget. HCAST-style: multi-hour SWE/cyber tasks with automatic checks.
items.how_graded: Automatic per-task scoring, then a logistic fit of success vs. human completion time gives the 50%/80% horizon.
items.fits_our_harness: Better as a METHOD than as a dataset. Josh can tag each of his frozen tasks with an estimated human completion time and plot pass rate vs. task length per model: a 'Vetted Bench time horizon' chart. Some RE-Bench tasks are public, but many HCAST tasks are held private. METR's May 2026 update puts Claude Mythos at a 50% horizon of likely 16 hours or more (80%: about 3h06m) and notes measurements above 16h are unreliable with the current suite, so METR's own suite is near its ceiling.

items.name: PaperBench (replicate an ML paper from scratch)
items.what_it_tests: Long-horizon research engineering: reading an ICML 2024 paper and building and running a codebase that reproduces its results. It covers 20 papers and 8,316 rubric leaves co-written with the papers' authors.
items.example_task: Given an ICML paper PDF, write the code, run the experiments and produce the results from scratch; the Code-Dev variant skips execution.
items.how_graded: A hierarchical author-approved rubric scored by an LLM judge (the judge itself was validated against humans).
items.fits_our_harness: The rubric is someone else's (author-co-developed), which fits the principle, but execution needs GPUs and hours per paper. Feasible locally only as Code-Dev on 1-2 small papers, graded by Josh's blind majority-vote AI judge against the frozen rubric. The 2025 paper's best was 21% vs. 41.4% for human experts; 2026 frontier results were not found.

grading_techniques: Hidden FAIL_TO_PASS + PASS_TO_PASS tests in a pinned Docker image (SWE-bench recipe). Hash the test files and image digest as the frozen answer key.
Harbor task format (Dockerfile + instruction + tests/ + oracle solution). The oracle run proves each task is solvable before freezing, and Harbor has native claude-code / codex agents.
Test-integrity guards against reward hacking (from FreshBrew and Terminal-Bench 2.1): assert that test count, assertions and coverage did not drop, and that test files are unchanged (hash check).

Scripted user-workflow replay: convert a benchmark's browser workflows (Vibe Code Bench, ViBench test plans, SWE-Lancer E2E) into deterministic Playwright scripts instead of an LLM browser agent, and score the fraction of substeps passed.
Two-stage 'build then extend your own code' (ViBench Vibe-on-Vibe) to measure compounding error; reuse stage-1 artifacts as stage-2 inputs.
Unit-test pass FRACTION as partial credit (Commit0) instead of binary pass/fail, which separates models on long builds.
Fresh-slice decontamination: draw tasks from issues created after model cutoffs (SWE-rebench / SWE-bench-Live monthly splits) and record the slice date in metadata.
Memorization probe: give the model only the task ID or repo+issue number and check whether it reproduces the gold patch (the OpenAI SWE-bench Verified audit method).
Rubric-tree LLM judging with author-written leaves and blind majority vote (PaperBench), for outputs scripts cannot decide.
METR-style time-horizon fit: tag each task with estimated human minutes, fit logistic success vs. log(time) per model, and report the 50%/80% horizon.
Multiple attempts with best/mean pass@1 and confidence intervals (SWE-rebench 5 runs; Scale reports plus/minus CIs) so small-N differences are not over-read.
Dollar-weighted scoring (SWE-Lancer), a viewer-legible aggregate for a video.
lanes.notes: Leaderboard numbers conflict a lot by source and scaffold. For SWE-Bench Pro, Scale's standardized public set top is 61.5 (Muse Spark 1.1), while vendor aggregators (llm-stats, BenchLM) claim 80-90% for Claude Opus 5.5 / Fable 5. The difference is self-reported scores on vendor scaffolds vs. a fixed scaffold. I read Scale's page directly; the BenchLM / llm-stats / CodingFleet figures come only from search snippets and are aggregator claims, so treat them cautiously. This is an argument for Josh's approach (same harness, same scaffold, frozen tasks). SWE-bench Verified is effectively dead (OpenAI Feb 2026 audit: flawed tests plus verbatim gold-patch recall). SWE-Bench Pro itself had leakage/flawed-task problems, fixed in 'Pro Verified' (arXiv 2609.08149); I only read the abstract, not task counts or scores. Vibe Code Bench v1.1 is about saturated at the top (about 90% for three Claude models). ViBench (Opus 4.6 46%) and METR's long horizon still separate models, but newer models have not been published on ViBench. Commit0, FEA/FeatBench, FreshBrew and SWE-Lancer lack verified 2026 frontier results, so they are marked 'separates' or 'unknown' from their 2025 papers only. Commit0 and FEA-style tasks use popular open-source repos, so contamination/memorization risk is high; prefer obscure repos, fresh splits, or a memorization probe. Practical local-run cost: SWE-bench / Terminal-Bench / SWE-Lancer images are multi-GB, and PaperBench and RE-Bench need GPUs, so for Josh's subscription-only local setup the best-value picks are, in order: Terminal-Bench 2.1 via Harbor, a few SWE-rebench fresh-month instances, ViBench PRDs + test plans (web builds with Playwright grading), FreshBrew migrations, and a small Commit0 lite library. For video appeal: ViBench/Vibe Code Bench app builds, SWE-bench Multimodal UI bugs, SWE-Lancer 'dollars earned', and a METR-style time-horizon chart over Josh's own suite.

lanes.lane: Creative and multimodal code generation, excluding games: SVG, shaders/3D, generative art, data viz, animation, music code, CAD, diagrams, slides

items.name: Pelican-on-a-bicycle SVG test (Simon Willison) plus its variants: Tom Gally's 30-prompt SVG set and Castillo's 8x6 animal-by-vehicle grid
items.what_it_tests: Spatial composition and object knowledge written as raw SVG code with no visual feedback: anatomy, how a bicycle works, how a rider sits on it.
items.example_task: 'Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle.' Stricter 2025 version: the bicycle must be mechanically plausible and the bird must be a California brown pelican in breeding plumage. Gally-style variants: 'an octopus operating a pipe organ', 'a starfish driving a bulldozer'.
items.how_graded: Willison: informal side-by-side grids judged by eye. Gally: visual comparison only. Castillo's 'pelicanmaxxing' study: 1,008 SVGs (8 animals x 6 vehicles x 7 models x 3 samples, temperature 1.0) scored by an LLM judge from 1 to 5 on animal quality, vehicle quality and action coherence.
items.fits_our_harness: Good fit, and cheap. Artifact: a single .svg per prompt. Deterministic probes first: valid XML, renders headless with resvg or Playwright, no external hrefs, non-empty bounding box. Then a blind VLM judge (majority of 3) on a frozen rubric with Castillo's three axes. To avoid contamination, freeze a private held-out grid of animal x vehicle pairs, for example 5 of each drawn with a fixed seed, and keep the original pelican only as a video hook. Take the 'correct answer defined by others' from Willison's canonical prompt text and Castillo's rubric axes.
items.recency: Ran from 2024 through 2026, including GPT-6 Astra runs reported in 2026. Gally set: Nov 2025. Pelicanmaxxing study: 2026 (it mentions GLM-5.2).

items.name: Design Arena (designarena.ai): crowdsourced boards for Website, UI Component, Data Visualization, SVG, Logo, 3D Asset, Slides, Video and Audio
items.what_it_tests: Human aesthetic preference ('taste') for design output across 20+ categories, including the landing-page and website category Josh asked about.
items.example_task: The user types a prompt such as 'a portfolio landing page with scroll-driven parallax'. Two anonymous models each build it, and the voter picks the better one.
items.how_graded: Human pairwise votes combined with a Bradley-Terry (Elo) rating. Reported snapshots: Website board led by GLM-5.2 at 1343, ahead of Claude Fable 5 at 1335. SVG board led by GPT-6 Astra at 1494. The spread is narrow among the top models.
items.fits_our_harness: We can't use the leaderboard itself as a grader. What we can take is its category taxonomy and its prompt style as a source of task families. In our harness: artifact = a static site folder. Deterministic checks = Playwright loads the page with zero console errors, runs Lighthouse, finds no horizontal scroll at 375px, and confirms that scroll-driven effects actually change computed styles or transforms across scroll positions. Taste = a blind pairwise VLM judge against a frozen reference set, reported alongside the arena rank as the external anchor.

items.name: LMArena WebDev Arena / Code Arena
items.what_it_tests: Building a whole interactive web app or page from a single prompt, judged on how it looks and behaves.
items.example_task: 'Build a landing page for a coffee brand with animated hero and scroll effects.' Two models build it side by side and the user votes.
items.how_graded: Human pairwise votes combined with Bradley-Terry scores. Reported as of 2026-09-25: 795,514 votes across 134 models. One 2026-07-31 snapshot: Claude Opus 5 at about 1704, with open-weight Kimi K3 within about 29 Elo.
items.fits_our_harness: Use it as the external validity anchor: show that our local rank ordering on web tasks agrees with WebDev Arena. It can't be the grader itself. The same Playwright, Lighthouse and scroll-probe plus VLM-judge pipeline applies as for Design Arena.

items.name: Artificial Analysis MicroEvals: community one-prompt showdowns, e.g. 'LLM Ultimate Challenge: Interactive GLSL Shader Art'
items.what_it_tests: Mixing languages in one artifact (HTML + Three.js + GLSL) and getting the math right on a fractal, plus interactive controls.
items.example_task: Render a Julia set with GLSL shaders inside Three.js. Required: smooth animation, an exact gradient palette (indigo, then magenta, orange, yellow), zoom and pan controls, and morphing driven by mouse position.
items.how_graded: Community thumbs-up votes on outputs shown side by side (16 models on this prompt). Several strong models received 0 votes.
items.fits_our_harness: Strong fit, because the prompt spells out checkable requirements. Artifact: index.html. Probes: the WebGL context exists, the shader compiles (check for console errors), and canvas pixels change between frames, which proves animation. Sample canvas pixels to confirm the hues lie inside the specified gradient palette. Simulate a wheel event and a drag, then assert the rendered pixels change, which checks zoom and pan. A VLM judge covers only the aesthetics. The MicroEval page supplies the canonical prompt text.
items.recency: 2025 (prompt id suggests Aug 2025); platform still live

items.name: Ball bouncing inside a spinning hexagon/heptagon (viral prompt; KCORES LLM Arena formalized it)
items.what_it_tests: Physics simulation (gravity, friction, collision with a rotating wall) combined with a real-time canvas render. The classic failure is treating the rotating wall as if it were stationary.
items.example_task: 'Write a program that shows a ball bouncing inside a spinning hexagon, affected by gravity and friction, bouncing off the rotating walls realistically.' KCORES version: 20 numbered balls whose digits show spin, inside a spinning heptagon.
items.how_graded: Community side-by-side video comparisons. KCORES runs each model 3 times, keeps the best output, and scores it with human evaluation plus a scoring script.
items.fits_our_harness: The visual version is near-saturated among frontier models (it went viral in early 2025), so it's weak as a separator. We could make it harder and deterministic by requiring the simulation to expose state, such as window.__SIM__.step(dt) and positions. Then assert invariants from a frozen key: no ball ever leaves the polygon over 10k steps, energy stays non-increasing when friction > 0, and relative velocity at the wall is reflected in the wall's rotating frame. That turns it into a correctness test rather than a matter of taste.

items.name: WorldCoder-Bench (Three.js 3D world synthesis with StateProbe)
items.what_it_tests: Browser-native 3D scenes in Three.js that must obey spatial and physical constraints and keep user-facing controls in sync with hidden runtime state. Groups: Simulation, Rendering, Application.
items.example_task: One of 2,026 expert-curated tasks, optionally with .glb assets: build an interactive 3D scene whose objects and controls behave according to a hidden behavioral contract.
items.how_graded: Execution-based. Headless Chromium runs the scene, which exposes window.__3D_STATE__. Scripted action sequences run, and state snapshots are checked against hidden contracts written by domain experts. The contracts are calibrated with mutation testing: injected bugs must be caught. Best model reported is GPT-5.4 at 27.8% verification coverage. No model exceeds 30%, and perturbed variants drop the best to 19.9%. Models reach about 66% affordance coverage (objects are present) but only about 26% transition coverage (interactions fail).
items.fits_our_harness: Best-in-class fit and the closest analogue to Josh's voxel game, which is the only task of his that separates models. Take tasks from the public WorldCoder-Dev split (200 tasks with contracts and reference outputs). Freeze the contract JSON as the answer key, hash it, and grade with our Playwright runner calling the state interface. Its mutation-testing idea is also worth reusing to validate our own graders.

items.name: BenchCAD (programmatic CAD in CadQuery) plus Text2CAD-Bench
items.what_it_tests: Writing parametric CAD code (CadQuery) that reproduces an industrial part from images or text, answering design QA, and editing code from instructions.
items.example_task: Given multi-view renders of a flanged bracket, write a CadQuery program whose solid matches it. Or edit a program so a hole pattern changes as instructed.
items.how_graded: Geometric metrics against ground truth: voxel IoU (primary), Chamfer and Hausdorff distance, Feature-F1, essential-operation recall, execution rate. QA uses ±5% tolerance or exact match. Evaluated on GPT-5.3, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro, o3 and open models, with clear gaps (e.g. Vision QA 0.587 for Gemini 3.1 Pro versus 0.442 for Kimi). Text2CAD-Bench reports that advanced CAD features remain a capability frontier.
items.fits_our_harness: Excellent fit. The data (17,900 programs, HF BenchCAD/BenchCAD) is CC-BY-4.0 and the evaluation code is MIT. Artifact: part.py (or .scad) exported to STEP/STL. Answer key: the reference solid. Grader: pip install cadquery, compute voxel IoU and Chamfer distance, and pass at IoU ≥ threshold. It's fully deterministic. One caveat from a 2026 comparison: OpenSCAD 'can certify broken parts as clean', so prefer CadQuery, or add a manifold check. Renders of the parts look good on screen.

items.name: ChartMimic / Plot2Code (chart image to matplotlib code)
items.what_it_tests: Reproducing a scientific chart as rendering code: 18 regular and 4 advanced chart types, 201 subcategories.
items.example_task: Given a figure from a paper (e.g. a grouped bar chart with error bars and an inset), write matplotlib code that reproduces it.
items.how_graded: The code is executed and scored with low-level element metrics (text, layout, type, color) plus a GPT-4V high-level score. Execution rate is also reported.
items.fits_our_harness: Easy to wrap (4,800 human-curated triplets, ICLR 2025, open on GitHub), but a 2025 follow-up paper explicitly notes 'performance saturation issues' on ChartMimic and Plot2Code for frontier models. Use it only as a cheap sanity lane, or take the hardest subset. Grader: run the code, diff the rendered PNG against the reference (SSIM plus extracted text/labels), and check data values via the matplotlib object tree.

items.name: VisEval (natural language + database to visualization)
items.what_it_tests: Turning an NL question plus a database into a correct, legal and readable chart. Builds on nvBench. Split into single-table and multi-table, easy to extra-hard.
items.example_task: 'Show the number of flights per airline for 2019 as a sorted bar chart', given a SQLite database.
items.how_graded: Automated multi-dimensional checks: validity (the code runs), legality (right chart type, and data matches the labeled ground truth, which covers 2,524 queries on 146 databases), and readability (MLLM-assessed).
items.fits_our_harness: Good fit for a 'data viz dashboard' lane that isn't a game. Artifact: a chart script plus the rendered PNG and a data JSON. Answer key: the labeled ground-truth data and the list of allowed chart types. Grade by extracting plotted data from the chart object or a Vega-Lite spec and comparing it exactly. A VLM judge covers readability only. Could be extended to an interactive D3 dashboard with Playwright probes for tooltips and filters.

items.name: Vision2Code (multi-domain image to code: charts, geometry, graphs, scientific imagery, documents, 3D scenes)
items.what_it_tests: Reconstructing many kinds of images as executable programs, without depending on reference code.
items.example_task: Given a geometry diagram or a 3D spatial scene image, write a program that renders an equivalent image.
items.how_graded: The program is rendered and scored against the source image by a VLM rater using dataset-specific rubrics, plus deterministic guardrails for severe semantic failures. Render success is reported separately from reconstruction quality.
items.fits_our_harness: A useful template for the grading pattern (render, then rubric VLM, then deterministic guardrails). Its 2,169 examples from 15 datasets could seed an 'image-to-code' lane where the reference image is the frozen answer key. The VLM-rater dependence means we need majority vote and judge-bias checks.

items.name: TikZ scientific figures: DaTikZ (v2 to v4) / Edit2TikZ
items.what_it_tests: Generating and editing LaTeX TikZ code for scientific figures from captions or images. The code must compile, and the figure must be semantically right.
items.example_task: From a caption such as 'a commutative diagram of four objects with labeled morphisms', write TikZ that compiles. Or apply an edit instruction to an existing figure.
items.how_graded: Compile rate, then image-similarity or VLM metrics against the reference figure, then edit correctness. Edit2TikZ (Aug 2026) reports that proprietary models compile and render only about 75% of examples and remain limited on restoration and edit correctness.
items.fits_our_harness: Good fit. Artifact: a .tex file. Stage 1: deterministic compilation with tectonic or pdflatex (pass/fail). Stage 2: rasterize and compare with the frozen reference PNG (SSIM, or DreamSim-style embedding). Stage 3: a VLM judge checks the edit instruction. Answer keys come from the published datasets.

items.name: MermaidSeqBench (NL to Mermaid sequence diagrams); related: DiagramEval, IGenBench (infographics)
items.what_it_tests: Turning a textual process description into correct diagram-as-code: syntax, logic, completeness, activations, error paths.
items.example_task: 'User logs in; auth service validates token; on failure return 401 and log to audit service', written as a Mermaid sequence diagram.
items.how_graded: LLM-as-judge on six 0 to 1 dimensions (Syntax, Mermaid Only, Logic, Completeness, Activation Handling, Error & Status Tracking). The authors used two judges, DeepSeek-V3 and GPT-OSS-120B, and found judge-dependent variance but no saturation. DiagramEval instead proposes graph-based metrics.
items.fits_our_harness: Can be made deterministic, which beats the paper's judge. Parse the Mermaid output (the mermaid-cli parse must succeed), extract the participants and ordered message edges as a graph, and compare with the frozen key graph (edge precision/recall plus order constraints). Data: HF ibm-research/MermaidSeqBench (132 core samples), eval code on GitHub. Visually dull on its own, but fine inside a 'breadth' montage.

items.name: SlidesGen-Bench (slide-deck generation); related: DECKBench, PPTAgent/PPTEval
items.what_it_tests: Turning a source document into a deck that keeps the content, looks good and stays editable.
items.example_task: Given a research paper or report, generate an editable .pptx (or HTML deck) presenting it.
items.how_graded: Closed-form metrics. Content: a QuizBank of 10 multiple-choice questions per source, answered by a VLM from the slides. Aesthetics: HSV color harmony, colorfulness, WCAG contrast, and visual rhythm via subband entropy plus RMSSD. Editability: PEI levels 0 to 5 from parsing the file structure. Reports Spearman 0.71 against human preference, versus 0.57 for an LLM judge. Tested products include Gamma, NotebookLM, Kimi, Zhipu, Skywork and PPTAgent.
items.fits_our_harness: Strong fit for a 'productivity artifact' lane. Artifact: a .pptx made via python-pptx, or reveal.js HTML. Answer key: a frozen quiz bank per source document plus editability requirements. Grader: port their open-source metrics (color, contrast, clutter computed deterministically, and a PEI parse of the XML), plus a VLM answering the frozen quiz from slide renders. Decks are also easy to show on video.

items.name: Manim / code-to-animation: ManiBench, ManimBench, Code2Video, Animation2Code
items.what_it_tests: Motion design and educational animation as code (Manim CE): version-correct APIs, timing, and animations that visually match the intent. The papers call these failure modes 'syntactic hallucination' and 'visual-logic drift'.
items.example_task: 'Animate the Pythagorean theorem proof: draw a right triangle, construct squares on each side, rearrange areas to show a²+b²=c²' as a Manim Scene.
items.how_graded: Render success rate plus visual similarity to the reference video. One 2026 paper reports a fine-tuned Qwen3-Coder-30B at 94% render success and 85.7% visual similarity, 3 points above GPT-4.1. ManiBench checks API or version correctness and temporal fidelity.
items.fits_our_harness: Fit with care. Artifact: scene.py rendered to MP4 at a pinned manim version. Deterministic checks: renders without error, duration is within a window, and required mobjects exist at key timestamps (hook into the Scene to dump its mobject list per frame). A VLM judge on sampled keyframes checks that the steps of the explanation appear in order. Animations make it very video-friendly.

items.name: Music as code: ABC-Eval (ABC notation); also LilyPond and Strudel (live-coding) datasets
items.what_it_tests: Understanding symbolic music and following musical instructions in text-based notation. Strudel work generates live-coded patterns that are rendered to MIDI.
items.example_task: 'Write a 16-bar melody in D Dorian, 6/8 time, ending on the tonic, in ABC notation.' Or a Strudel pattern with a specified drum groove and chord progression.
items.how_graded: ABC-Eval has 1,086 samples across 10 subtasks (syntax comprehension through sequence-level reasoning), scored as QA or instruction-following accuracy. The Strudel dataset executes programs in the Strudel runtime to obtain MIDI.
items.fits_our_harness: Good deterministic fit for constraint-style music tasks. Artifact: .abc or a Strudel program. Parse it with music21 (or render to MIDI), then assert the frozen constraints: key and mode pitch set, meter, bar count, final note, chord progression, tempo. Taste can't be scripted, so optionally add a blind listening judge. Audio playback also makes a good video beat.

grading_techniques: Render and probe: headless Playwright or Chromium loads the artifact, then asserts zero console errors, that a WebGL context exists, that canvas pixels change between frames (animation is real), and that scroll or wheel events change computed styles/transforms (scroll-driven effects are real). Directly applicable to the portfolio/landing-page lane Josh asked about.

Exposed-state contracts (WorldCoder StateProbe): require the artifact to expose window.__STATE__ or a similar hook, drive scripted actions, and diff state snapshots against a hidden, frozen behavioral contract. This turns '3D scene or physics looks right' into a pass/fail check.

Mutation-testing the grader (from WorldCoder): inject known bugs into a reference solution, such as stale updates, swapped constants or a static wall. Reject any contract or probe that doesn't catch them. This validates our own answer keys.
Geometric metrics for CAD and 3D: voxel IoU, Chamfer and Hausdorff distance against the frozen reference solid (BenchCAD). Fully deterministic once the output is exported to STL/STEP.

Compile gate, then image similarity: tectonic/pdflatex for TikZ, resvg for SVG, mermaid-cli parse, a pinned manim render. Then compare to the reference PNG with SSIM or an embedding distance. Report 'render success' separately from 'quality' (Vision2Code and TikZ practice).

Structure extraction instead of pixels: parse Mermaid into a graph and compare edges; read plotted data from the chart's object tree or Vega-Lite spec (VisEval legality); parse the .pptx XML to get an editability level (SlidesGen PEI); parse ABC/MIDI with music21 to check key, meter and bar constraints.

Closed-form aesthetic metrics (SlidesGen-Bench): HSV color harmony, WCAG contrast, subband-entropy clutter. Cheaper and more reproducible than an LLM judge, and they reported Spearman 0.71 with humans versus 0.57 for an LLM judge.
Quiz-bank content fidelity: freeze N multiple-choice questions per source document, have a VLM answer them from renders of the artifact alone, and score accuracy.
Blind VLM judge with a frozen rubric and majority vote, for taste only. Use per-axis scores (e.g. Castillo's subject / vehicle / action-coherence 1-5), and shuffle model identity and ordering.

Anti-contamination prompt grids: instead of one famous prompt, use a seeded held-out grid (animal x vehicle, shape x physics variant) and report both the canonical prompt and the grid score (the pelicanmaxxing method).
External-anchor validation: check that our local rank order on web and design tasks correlates with the public Design Arena and WebDev Arena Bradley-Terry rankings.
lanes.notes:
- **Frontier status.**
  - Hard-unsolved: only WorldCoder-Bench has strong public evidence of this (best is GPT-5.4 at 27.8%, no model above 30%). It is the closest analogue to Josh's voxel game, which is the only task of his that separates models.
  - Measurable gaps reported: BenchCAD and Edit2TikZ (about 75% compile rate for proprietary models).
  - Near-saturated or explicitly saturated: ChartMimic/Plot2Code and the viral bouncing-ball-in-hexagon prompt.
  - Human arenas: Design Arena and WebDev Arena show narrow Elo spreads among top models (a few dozen points), so they separate models but only weakly at the very top.
- **Contamination.** The pelican prompt is famous enough that labs could train on it. Castillo's 2026 grid study found little evidence of this (the pelican-bicycle cell ranked 42nd of 48). It is still safer to use private held-out variants and keep the canonical prompt only as a video hook.
- **Judge bias.**
  - MermaidSeqBench found judge-dependent scores: DeepSeek-V3 was more lenient than GPT-OSS-120B.
  - SlidesGen-Bench found an LLM judge correlates with humans worse than closed-form metrics (0.57 vs 0.71).
  - Vision2Code relies on a VLM rater with guardrails.
  - Rule: never use the model under test as a judge, and prefer deterministic probes first.
- **Leaderboard numbers are volatile and aggregator-sourced.**
  - Design Arena, WebDev Arena and SVG boards were quoted via third-party aggregators (benchlm.ai, modelgrep, ainexhub); I couldn't load Design Arena's own ranking tables (the leaderboard page only showed categories).
  - The llm-stats 'SVG-Bench' is described as an internal benchmark with a single self-reported result (MiniMax M3, 0.637), so it is not credible as an answer key.
  - Treat every Elo number as a snapshot, not ground truth.
- **Unverified items.**
  - I did not open the MicroEvals voting rules in depth; the page only shows thumbs-up counts, and it is community voting on single outputs.
  - The KCORES rubric details aren't spelled out in its README.
  - The WorldCoder repo is an anonymous 4open.science link from a June 2026 arXiv paper; it may move once the paper is de-anonymized.
- **Not found as a named benchmark.** I found no credible dedicated 'scroll-animation portfolio site' benchmark. That lane is best built from the Design Arena / WebDev Arena prompt style plus our own Playwright scroll probes, with the arena rank as the external 'defined by others' anchor.
- **Shadertoy-style GLSL.** Apart from the MicroEvals prompt, I found no public frontier benchmark; searches returned kernel benchmarks such as KernelBench, not visual shaders.
- **Where a public answer key exists.** For the 'correct answer defined by other people' principle, the strongest candidates are:
  - BenchCAD (CC-BY data, MIT eval code)
  - MermaidSeqBench (HF dataset plus eval code)
  - SlidesGen-Bench (open code plus human-preference set)
  - the WorldCoder-Dev split (200 tasks with contracts)
  - ChartMimic and VisEval (labeled ground truth)

lanes.lane: Knowledge work and tool-use agent benchmarks (GDPval, tau2, BrowseComp, WebArena, OSWorld, spreadsheets, slides, deep research, MCP/tool calling, long-horizon business sims)

items.name: GDPval (OpenAI) / GDPval-AA v2.1 (Artificial Analysis)
items.what_it_tests: Knowledge work that produces real deliverables across 44 occupations and 9 industries: documents, slides, spreadsheets, diagrams built from reference files
items.example_task: Given a client's financial files, produce a formatted .xlsx model plus a .docx memo, the way a financial analyst would for a real client
items.how_graded: Original: blind pairwise grading by industry experts against a human expert deliverable. GDPval-AA: blind pairwise LLM judge, aggregated into Elo (anchored so DeepSeek V4.1 Flash = 1600). Models run with shell and web in an agent loop ('Stirrup'). The 220-task gold set is public on HF (openai/gdpval)
items.fits_our_harness: Strong fit and the best 'correct answer is defined by other people' source in this lane. Take 3-5 public gold tasks with their reference files. Artifact = the .docx/.xlsx/.pptx the agent writes to disk. Answer key = the published expert deliverable, frozen and hashed. Grader = deterministic probes first (file opens, required sheets and sections exist, key numbers match within tolerance), then a blind pairwise AI judge (majority of 3) comparing model output with the expert deliverable. This mirrors the official method
items.recency: Dataset from late 2025. AA leaderboard updated 2026-09-22, top Elo is Claude Opus 5.5 at 1846. GDPval-MM multimodal variant is also tracked

items.name: tau-bench / tau2-bench (Sierra)
items.what_it_tests: Customer-support agents: multi-turn chat with a simulated user plus domain tools (airline, retail, telecom) under policy constraints. Includes a voice full-duplex mode
items.example_task: A simulated airline customer asks to change a basic-economy flight. The agent must follow the policy doc, call the booking tools correctly and refuse what the policy forbids
items.how_graded: Deterministic: the final database state is compared with the gold end state, plus required outputs. pass^k measures reliability over repeated trials
items.fits_our_harness: Good fit. It is open source (sierra-research/tau2-bench) and runs locally. The simulated user needs an LLM, which adds a variable, so fix one cheap model as the user sim for every run. Artifact = transcript plus final DB JSON. Answer key = the official gold DB state per task. Grader = the official evaluator, or a port of its DB-diff. Running pass^k (e.g. 4 runs each) makes a good 'reliability' video angle. Needs an adapter that exposes the tools as MCP/CLI to Claude Code and Codex
items.recency: Active repo with a taubench.com leaderboard. Airline leader Gemini 3.7 Flash at 80.6% (OpenRouter, 2026-09-26)

items.name: BrowseComp (OpenAI) / BrowseComp-Plus
items.what_it_tests: Hard multi-hop web research for short, verifiable answers ('inverted questions' that are easy to check and hard to find)
items.example_task: Identify a paper from constraints such as 'published between 2018 and 2023 at a venue in X, third author's advisor did Y'. Answer is one short string
items.how_graded: Exact or normalized short-answer match against the key (the official version uses an LLM grader for equivalence). BrowseComp-Plus pins a fixed document corpus so runs are reproducible and fair
items.fits_our_harness: Partly. Original BrowseComp needs the live web, which drifts and can leak answers (answers are online), and the top scores are within about 1 point of each other. BrowseComp-Plus (fixed corpus, local retriever) fits the harness well: artifact = answer.txt, key = official answer, grader = normalized string match plus an LLM equivalence check. Useful for a 'deep research' segment but not a separator
items.recency: 2025 release. Sept 2026 leaderboards: top about 92.5% (Atria Dawn Preview), GPT-5.6 Sol 92.2%. Trackers call it nearing saturation. BrowseComp-Plus accepted at ACL 2026

items.name: DeepResearch Bench (RACE + FACT)
items.what_it_tests: Long-form research report writing: 100 PhD-level tasks (50 EN / 50 ZH) across 22 fields. Tests report quality, citation accuracy and retrieval
items.example_task: Write a cited research report on a technical or economic question, e.g. market structure analysis in a named industry
items.how_graded: RACE: reference-based LLM judge with dynamic per-task criteria weighting against a reference report. FACT: extracts claim-citation pairs and checks that the cited URL supports each claim. Official judge switched to GPT-5.5 in May 2026, with separate legacy and new leaderboards
items.fits_our_harness: Fits as an 'AI judge' tier task. Artifact = report.md with URLs. Answer key = the official reference reports and criteria (public in the repo). Grader = run the official RACE script, or reimplement it with your blind majority-vote judge; FACT citation checks can be partly scripted (fetch URL, check the claim). Caveat: a live web makes it non-deterministic, so freeze the date and accept variance

items.name: OSWorld / OSWorld-Verified (and OSWorld 2.0)
items.what_it_tests: Computer use: GUI agents doing real desktop tasks in Ubuntu/Windows VMs (LibreOffice, Chrome, GIMP, VS Code, multi-app workflows)
items.example_task: In LibreOffice Calc, highlight rows where column D exceeds the average, then export to PDF on the Desktop
items.how_graded: Execution-based: per-task scripts inspect the final VM and file state (cell values, file existence, settings)
items.fits_our_harness: Weak fit. It needs VM snapshots and a screenshot/action loop, which Claude Code and Codex CLI don't do natively (their harnesses are shell-first). A shell agent can also often bypass the GUI, which defeats the point. The top systems have passed the 72.36% human baseline (Qwen3.8 Max 86.1%). Better use: borrow the pattern, i.e. 'final-state checker scripts on files', for a local LibreOffice-headless task
items.recency: OSWorld-Verified leaderboard updated Sept 2026. Steel.dev tracks OSWorld 2.0

items.name: WebArena / WebArena-Verified (ServiceNow) / VisualWebArena
items.what_it_tests: Browser agents on 812 tasks in self-hosted clones of e-commerce, CMS admin, GitLab, Reddit-like forum and maps sites
items.example_task: On the self-hosted shop admin, find the top-selling product in Q1 and change its price by 10%
items.how_graded: WebArena-Verified uses deterministic evaluators on the agent's response and captured network traces, instead of the original brittle string and LLM checks
items.fits_our_harness: Possible but heavy: Docker images for about 5 sites. Claude Code and Codex would need Playwright MCP to browse. Artifact = answer plus network trace, key = verified evaluator config. Important: agents have read answers via file:// URLs in the task configs, so the harness must keep evaluator files out of the agent sandbox. Better as a later 'platform' addition than an early video task

items.name: SpreadsheetBench (v1 Verified) and SpreadsheetBench 2
items.what_it_tests: Real spreadsheet manipulation drawn from Excel forum questions (v1). End-to-end business spreadsheet workflows (v2)
items.example_task: Given a workbook, write formulas that fill column F with the per-region running total and flag duplicates, keeping the existing formatting
items.how_graded: Deterministic cell-level comparison of the output workbook against an answer workbook (openpyxl), in some cases over multiple test-case variants of the input
items.fits_our_harness: Excellent fit and cheap. The agent edits an .xlsx on disk with Python/openpyxl or LibreOffice headless. Answer key = the official answer workbook, frozen and hashed. Grader = a script that diffs target cells, plus recalculation via LibreOffice to catch hardcoded values instead of formulas. v1 is saturated (top 94.75%), so use SpreadsheetBench 2 tasks (top 34.8%), which clearly separate models
items.recency: v1 Verified leaderboards 2026. SpreadsheetBench 2 paper June 2026 (arXiv 2606.29955)

items.name: Slide generation: PPTEval / PresentBench / SlidesBench / PPT-Eval
items.what_it_tests: Making presentation decks from a source document or instruction: content, design, coherence. PPT-Eval (2026) targets computer-use agents on PowerPoint editing
items.example_task: Turn this 12-page research paper into a 10-slide .pptx deck for a non-expert audience with charts and speaker notes
items.how_graded: PresentBench: instance-specific rubrics scored by an MLLM judge (stricter and better aligned with humans). PPTEval: MLLM scores for Content/Design/Coherence. SlidesBench: reference-based similarity plus design metrics
items.fits_our_harness: Good visual video task. Artifact = deck.pptx, rendered to PNGs through LibreOffice headless. Answer key = the published PresentBench per-instance rubric, frozen. Grader = deterministic probes (slide count, notes present, no text overflow via python-pptx bounding boxes, images load), then a blind multimodal judge on the rendered slides, majority of 3 against the rubric. Very watchable side-by-side
items.recency: PresentBench and SlidesGen-Bench 2026. PPT-Eval arXiv June 2026. SLATE Sept 2026

items.name: Toolathlon / Toolathlon-Verified (HKUST)
items.what_it_tests: Long-horizon multi-app tool use: 32 apps and 604 tools (Calendar, Notion, WooCommerce, Kubernetes, BigQuery, email), about 20 steps per task
items.example_task: Read unfilled orders in WooCommerce, email each customer a delay notice, and log them in a Notion table
items.how_graded: Execution-based: dedicated scripts check the final state of the systems (emails sent, records updated)
items.fits_our_harness: Medium fit. Environments are containerized MCP servers, and Claude Code and Codex speak MCP natively, so the adapter is natural. Artifact = final system state dump. Key/grader = the official per-task check scripts. Cost is standing up several containers; pick 5-10 tasks that need only local services (filesystem, SQLite, local email mock). Wide spread between models (about 58-78% depending on the tracker)

items.name: MCPMark / MCPMark-Verified and MCP-Universe (Salesforce)
items.what_it_tests: Stress-tests real MCP-server use (GitHub, Notion, Postgres, filesystem, Playwright) with verifiable CRUD-heavy tasks
items.example_task: Using the Postgres MCP, migrate a schema, add an index and backfill a derived column so a given query returns the expected rows
items.how_graded: Programmatic verification scripts on the resulting environment state
items.fits_our_harness: Good fit. MCP is the native tool channel of Claude Code, Codex and pi, so it exercises the harness itself. Filesystem and Postgres tasks run fully locally in Docker. Artifact = DB or filesystem state. Key = official verifier. Grader = the verifier script run outside the agent sandbox. MCPMark (non-verified) top is about 60.8%, a good separator. Verified top is about 81%

items.name: Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL v4)
items.what_it_tests: Raw function-calling accuracy: picking the right function, correct argument types and values, no hallucinated functions. Covers single, parallel, multi-turn and agentic (web search, memory) categories
items.example_task: Given 5 function schemas and a user request, emit the exact call(s) with correct arguments, or correctly abstain
items.how_graded: Deterministic AST matcher against a reference call, plus executable checks for some categories
items.fits_our_harness: Poor fit for a CLI coding-agent harness. BFCL measures a model's raw tool-call emission through an API, whereas Claude Code and Codex wrap tool calling in their own scaffold. It could be done as a 'write calls.json' task, but that turns it into a formatting test. Better cited as context than run. Leaderboard last updated 2026-04-12

items.name: TheAgentCompany (CMU)
items.what_it_tests: Consequential work tasks inside a simulated software company: self-hosted GitLab, OwnCloud, Plane and RocketChat with simulated coworkers. Admin, finance, HR, PM and SWE tasks
items.example_task: Collect the expense receipts from OwnCloud, reconcile them against the policy spreadsheet, and message the finance coworker on RocketChat with the discrepancies
items.how_graded: Checkpoint-based evaluators with partial credit: scripted state checks plus LLM checks for some free-form outputs
items.fits_our_harness: Medium-heavy. Fully self-hostable (Docker) and gives partial credit, which works well on screen as a progress bar. Artifact = end states and messages. Key = the official checkpoints. The published leaderboard looks stale (Claude 3.7 Sonnet 52.7%), so frontier status in 2026 is unclear, which is itself a reason to run it fresh. Pick the finance and admin tasks that avoid the heavy browser use
items.recency: NeurIPS 2025 D&B. The public leaderboard appears not updated for 2026 models

items.name: Vending-Bench 2 (Andon Labs)
items.what_it_tests: Long-horizon coherence: running a simulated vending business for a year (inventory, supplier email negotiation, pricing, fees, disruptions)
items.example_task: Start with $500 and a vending machine. Maximize the bank balance after 365 simulated days
items.how_graded: A single objective metric: final money balance, averaged over runs with variance
items.fits_our_harness: Concept fits and is very video-friendly (a dollar number and an equity curve), but the official environment is Andon Labs-run rather than a public local package. Options: (a) cite the published leaderboard, or (b) build a small 'Vetted Vend' sim yourself, though that breaks the 'answer defined by other people' rule unless you copy their published rules exactly. Large spread (GPT-6 Astra $15.5k vs Claude Opus 5 $11.2k vs GLM-5.2 $8.3k)

items.name: Finance spreadsheet workflows: MBABench / WorkstreamBench and OmegaUse-OfficeVal
items.what_it_tests: End-to-end finance and office-suite workflows (building models, multi-file reporting) with economic grounding
items.example_task: Build a 3-statement model from the provided 10-K extracts and answer valuation questions in a summary sheet
items.how_graded: Mix of cell- and answer-level checks plus rubric judging (per the papers)
items.fits_our_harness: Candidate pool for harder GDPval-style xlsx tasks with published answer keys. Check each paper's release license and data before freezing. Same grader pattern as SpreadsheetBench (cell diff plus LibreOffice recalculation) plus a judge for narrative cells

grading_techniques: Final-state diffing: grade the environment state (DB rows, files, cells, sent emails), not the transcript. Used by tau2, OSWorld, Toolathlon, MCPMark and WebArena-Verified
Cell-level workbook comparison with openpyxl, after recalculating in headless LibreOffice so hardcoded numbers can't pass as formulas

Render-then-judge for office artifacts: convert .pptx/.docx to PNG/PDF with LibreOffice headless, run deterministic probes (text overflow via python-pptx bounds, slide count, broken images), then a blind multimodal judge with an instance-specific rubric (PresentBench style)
Blind pairwise comparison against an expert reference deliverable, aggregated into Elo or win-rate (GDPval / GDPval-AA). Randomize A/B order and take a majority vote to reduce position bias
pass^k reliability: run the same task k times and report the share where all k succeed (tau-bench). This separates 'can' from 'reliably does'
